core: What the chain of infection is: six conditions that must line up for an infection to spread (CDC framing)
The six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host
The reservoir idea: where germs live — people, animals, surfaces, water
Breaking the chain: hand hygiene, PPE, cleaning, vaccines, isolation as link-specific counters
Why the chain matters: one broken link stops the spread
Honest framing: the chain as a checklist for every infection, not a guarantee
supporting: Factors that raise host susceptibility (underlying illness, certain medications, catheters and procedures)
Carriers and colonization: spreading germs without symptoms
outOfScope: Infection control programs and policy (own topic: infection-control)
Hand hygiene technique and the WHO 5 Moments (own topic: hand-hygiene)
Transmission-based precautions, isolation categories, PPE donning/doffing (own topic: transmission-based-precautions)

claims.claim: An infection occurs when germs enter the body, increase in number, and cause a reaction in the body.

The chain of infection is the sequence in which an infectious agent leaves its reservoir through a portal of exit, is conveyed by some mode of transmission, and enters through an appropriate portal of entry to infect a susceptible host; all links must be present for infection to spread.
Reservoirs of infectious agents include humans, animals, and the environment, and the reservoir may or may not be the source from which an agent is transferred to a host.
Germs are microorganisms found in air, soil, water, and on and in the human body; the main types are bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites.
In healthcare settings germs travel by contact (touching), sprays and splashes (droplets that travel a short distance, within about 6 feet), inhalation of airborne particles, and sharps injuries.

Droplet spread occurs through relatively large, short-range aerosols produced by sneezing, coughing, or talking; airborne transmission occurs when infectious agents are carried by dust or droplet nuclei suspended in air.

A susceptible person is someone who is not vaccinated or otherwise immune, or who has a weakened immune system, with a way for germs to enter the body; underlying conditions (e.g., diabetes, cancer), certain medications, and medical devices such as catheters can increase susceptibility.

Control measures are usually directed against the segment of the infection chain most susceptible to intervention: for example, isolation to interrupt direct transmission, decontamination or removal of vehicles, and treatment of infected people to clear the agent.

Handwashing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, alcohol-based hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol, covering coughs, staying home when sick, and cleaning frequently touched surfaces help protect against germs.

conflictingEvidence.issue: CDC materials frame the spread of infection two ways: a three-part version (source, susceptible person, transmission) and the full six-link chain.
positions: CDC's How Infections Spread page presents three necessary conditions: source, susceptible person, and transmission.
CDC's Principles of Epidemiology Lesson 1, Section 10 presents the complete six-link chain: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The six-link chain is the fuller version of the same idea; the three-part framing is a simplification of it. This lesson teaches the six links and notes the shorter framing only where it aids understanding.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Terminology: the CDC chain materials use both 'reservoir' and 'source' for where a germ comes from.
positions: Some materials use 'source' loosely for any place germs are found (including sinks and surfaces).
Principles of Epidemiology distinguishes reservoir (where the agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies) from source (where the agent was transferred from in a particular case).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the precise distinction and includes the CDC's botulism example (soil is the reservoir; improperly canned food is the source), avoiding the loose usage.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No generated draft existed for this topic in the phase-4 content store at write time (public/content/phase-4/lessons.json contained no chain-of-infection entry), so there were no draft claims to carry over or reject.
correctionsNeeded: None — no prior draft to correct; all lesson content was written from verified Tier A sources and original examples.
rightsIssues: All three sources are U.S. government works (CDC; NLM/MedlinePlus) used as reference only; no source prose reproduced; all examples and wording in the lesson are original.

sourceRecords.title: How Infections Spread
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Division of Healthcare Quality Promotion
sourceRecords.notes: cdc.gov blocks direct fetch; read via Internet Archive Wayback Machine capture 20240202212128 of the live URL (page last reviewed January 7, 2016). Supports: an infection occurs when germs enter the body, multiply, and cause a reaction; three necessary conditions (source, susceptible person, transmission); transmission by contact (touch), sprays and splashes within about 6 feet, inhalation of airborne particles, and sharps injuries; examples (MRSA/VRE, pertussis, TB, measles, HIV/HBV/HCV); factors that increase susceptibility (diabetes, cancer, organ transplant, certain medications, urinary catheters and surgery); environmental sources of germs (bed rails, medical equipment, sinks, faucets, cooling towers, indwelling devices).

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition — Lesson 1, Section 10: Chain of Infection
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly at archive.cdc.gov (CDC's own archive host; live cdc.gov URL www.cdc.gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section10.html). Supports: the chain of infection definition (agent leaves its reservoir through a portal of exit, is conveyed by a mode of transmission, and enters through a portal of entry to infect a susceptible host); reservoirs include humans, animals, and the environment; the reservoir may or may not be the source (botulism: soil is the reservoir, improperly canned food the source); portals of exit (respiratory, stool, skin lesions, blood); modes of transmission (direct contact, droplet spread, airborne, vehicle, vector); portals of entry (respiratory, fecal-oral, skin, mucous membranes, blood); susceptible host (specific immunity from infection or vaccine, nonspecific defenses, malnutrition and illness raising susceptibility); control measures target the segment most susceptible to intervention (isolation, decontamination, treatment).
